study_identification.title: Individualized gray matter morphological abnormalities unveil two neuroanatomical obsessive-compulsive disorder subtypes

study_characteristics.study_objective: To identify distinct OCD subtypes based on individualized gray matter morphological abnormalities using normative modeling, and to examine their disease epicenters and associations with neurotransmitter receptor/transporter distributions.

dataset_name.answer: Healthy controls recruited from community via poster advertisements at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University; External structural covariance network dataset from Southwest University (Wei et al., 2018 - 492 healthy individuals aged 19-80 years)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: CAT12 toolbox; voxel-based morphometry; bias field correction; brain segmentation into gray/white matter and CSF; partial volume effect correction; normalization to MNI space; resampling to 1.5 mm³; nonlinear modulation; smoothing with 6-mm FWHM Gaussian kernel; Brainnetome atlas (246 regions)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Image Quality Rating (IQR) recorded. No significant differences in IQR between HCs and OCD patients (HC mean 2.09 ± 0.15, OCD mean 2.09 ± 0.16, p = 0.976).

software_tool.answer: GAUSSIAN PROCESS REGRESSION AND CLASSIFICATION Toolbox version 4.2 (http://www.GaussianProcess.org/gpml/code)

response_variable.answer: Gray matter volume (GMV) for 246 regions based on Brainnetome atlas

predictor_effects.answer: Not explicitly specified as fixed or random effects

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The paper controls for sex, age, and TIV as covariates in group comparisons, and uses IQR for quality control. However, the study is single-site, so site effects are not explicitly addressed. The normative model accounts for age and sex as predictors, but details on how variance heteroscedasticity or other nuisance structures are handled in the GPR model are not fully specified.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Subsequently, for each subtype, we examined the gray matter morphological abnormalities relative to HCs using a two-sample t-test, with sex, age, and TIV as covariates. ... To ensure data quality, the Image Quality Rating (IQR) was recorded.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The paper does not describe any within-sample validation strategy such as cross-validation using the same dataset. The normative model is trained on healthy controls and applied to OCD patients, but no explicit validation metrics (e.g., EV, MSLL, RHO, skewness, kurtosis) on the training set are reported.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: No explicit mention of within-sample validation metrics or cross-validation procedures in the methods or results sections.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The paper does not describe testing the normative model on an independent healthy control sample from the same domain. All healthy controls (N=106) appear to be used for model training, with no independent test set mentioned.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No mention of holding out an independent HC test set or external validation on independent HC samples.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The paper does not validate the normative model on data from a different domain (e.g., different scanner, site, or cohort). The study is conducted at a single site with a single scanner (3-Tesla GE Discovery MR750).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: High-resolution T1-weighted anatomical images of participants were acquired using on 3-Tsela GE Discovery MR750 scanner (General Electric, Fairfield Connecticut, USA)

clinical_dataset.answer: OCD patients recruited from outpatient services within the Department of Psychiatry at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University

clinical_groups_age.answer: OCD overall: mean 22.93 (sd 9.31); Subtype 1: mean 21.49 (sd 9.12); Subtype 2: mean 24.31 (sd 9.38)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (positive Z scores indicate higher GMVs in patients compared to HCs, negative Z scores indicate lower GMVs). Z-score vectors (246 × 1) for each patient used as features for clustering.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: K-means clustering algorithm with squared Euclidean distance (optimal number determined by silhouette values); Two-sample t-tests with FDR correction for group comparisons (sex, age, TIV as covariates); Chi-square tests and two-sample t-tests for demographic comparisons between subtypes; Structural covariance network analysis (Pearson's correlation between regional abnormalities and SC-informed abnormalities); Disease epicenter mapping via permutation testing (10,000 iterations); Multilinear regression models linking neurotransmitter receptor/transporter profiles to gray matter abnormalities (permutation testing with FDR correction); Dominance analysis to assess relative importance of neurotransmitter predictors.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Two distinct OCD subtypes were identified with opposite patterns of gray matter abnormalities (subtype 1: increased GMV; subtype 2: decreased GMV), divergent disease epicenters (subtype 1: middle frontal gyrus; subtype 2: striatum, thalamus, hippocampus), and distinct associations with neurotransmitter receptors (subtype 1: 5HT1A; subtype 2: 5HT2A).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Using normative modeling and k-means clustering on individualized GMV Z-scores, two robust OCD subtypes were identified. Subtype 1 (N=49, 73.47% male) showed significantly increased GMV in frontal gyrus, precuneus, insula, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, and temporal gyrus (FDR corrected p < 0.05). Subtype 2 (N=51, 33.33% male) exhibited significantly decreased GMV in frontal gyrus, precuneus, insula, superior parietal gyrus, temporal gyrus, and fusiform (FDR corrected p < 0.05). When all patients were combined, no significant GMV differences emerged compared to HCs. Reproducibility analyses showed high consistency: average ARI = 0.98 (±0.04) for subsample validation, ARI = 0.74 between different brain atlases, and ARI = 0.62 for different distance metrics. Structural covariance network analysis revealed significant correlations between regional abnormalities and SC-informed abnormalities (subtype 1: r = 0.44, p_FDR < 0.001; subtype 2: r = 0.50, p_FDR < 0.001). Disease epicenters differed: subtype 1 showed epicenters in middle frontal gyrus (permutation p < 0.01), while subtype 2 displayed epicenters in striatum, thalamus, and hippocampus (permutation p < 0.01). Multilinear models linking neurotransmitter profiles to GMV abnormalities showed adjusted R² = 0.43 for subtype 1 and R² = 0.34 for subtype 2 (all FDR-corrected permutation p < 0.001). Dominance analysis identified 5HT1A as most significant for subtype 1, and 5HT2A for subtype 2. Despite substantial structural differences, subtypes showed indistinguishable clinical profiles (Y-BOCS, illness duration, age of onset all p > 0.05), except for sex distribution (χ² = 16.161, p < 0.001).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: First, cross-sectional design limits assessment of subtype stability and generalizability; longitudinal validation needed. Second, limited clinical information restricted exploration of differences in other clinical aspects beyond Y-BOCS; comprehensive clinical data needed in future studies. Third, neurotransmitter-structural abnormality associations based on group-level PET atlases may not capture individual variations in neurotransmitter systems. Fourth, OCD patients had significantly lower educational levels than HCs (p < 0.001), though no differences between subtypes were found, suggesting minimal impact on clustering results.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The identified subtypes may exhibit distinct treatment responses to serotonergic medications given their differential associations with 5HT1A vs. 5HT2A receptors, which could be explored in future research. The findings suggest that inconsistent results in previous OCD neuroimaging literature may stem from differing subtype proportions across studies. The network-based spreading model is supported, with distinct disease epicenters suggesting different pathological progression trajectories. Authors note potential for future multivariate correlation analyses between neuroimaging features and clinical characteristics, and investigation of individualized abnormalities to predict prognosis.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is notable for its focus on OCD subtyping using normative modeling of gray matter volume rather than traditional case-control approaches. Key methodological features: (1) Single-site study with first-episode, untreated OCD patients ensuring sample homogeneity; (2) Use of Brainnetome atlas (246 regions) for primary analysis, with AAL atlas (90 regions) for validation; (3) External dataset (N=492 HCs from Southwest University, Wei et al., 2018) used specifically for constructing structural covariance network, separate from normative model training; (4) Comprehensive sensitivity analyses including subsample validation, alternative atlases, and alternative distance metrics; (5) Integration of PET-derived neurotransmitter receptor/transporter atlas from Hansen et al. (2022) covering 19 receptor/transporter types; (6) Disease epicenter mapping methodology adapted from previous psychiatric neuroimaging studies (Shafiei et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024); (7) All patients were Han Chinese, right-handed, and underwent rigorous exclusion criteria; (8) Scanner specifications: 3T GE Discovery MR750, TR=8164ms, TE=3.18ms, TI=900ms, flip angle=7°, 256×256 matrix, 188 slices, 1mm thickness, 1×1×1mm³ voxels; (9) The study represents an application of precision psychiatry approaches to OCD heterogeneity, moving beyond symptom-based subtyping to neurobiologically-informed classification.
